title: The Bald Man and the Fly
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Fly settled on the head of a Bald Man and bit him. In his eagerness to kill it, he hit himself a smart slap. But the Fly escaped, and said to him in derision, "You tried to kill me for just one little bite; what will you do to yourself now, for the heavy smack you have just given yourself?"

"Oh, for that blow I bear no grudge," he replied, "for I never intended myself any harm; but as for you, you contemptible insect, who live by sucking human blood, I'd have borne a good deal more than that for the satisfaction of dashing the life out of you!"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Fly settle at the start?
options: On a windowsill nearby
On a piece of fruit
On the head of a Bald Man
On the Bald Man's hand

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Bald Man do in his eagerness to kill the Fly?
options: He hits himself a smart slap
He swats at the air repeatedly
He runs to find a fly swatter
He calls out for someone to help him

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to the Fly after the Bald Man slaps himself?
options: The Fly is killed instantly
The Fly is badly injured but survives
The Fly is trapped under the Man's hand
The Fly escapes

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fly say in derision to the Man?
options: That he should give up trying to catch flies
That he hurt himself worse than the Fly's bite
That he will never catch the Fly now
That bald men always miss their targets

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Man feel about the blow he gave himself?
options: He is furious with himself for missing the Fly
He regrets it deeply and vows never to try again
He bears no grudge, since he never intended himself any harm
He blames the Fly entirely for the pain

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Man call the Fly?
options: "You contemptible insect"
"You clever creature"
"You foolish pest"
"You tiny nuisance"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what would the Man have been willing to endure for the satisfaction of killing the Fly?
options: Nothing at all, since it isn't worth the trouble
Only the same amount of pain, no more
A much smaller amount of pain than he felt
A good deal more than the smack he gave himself

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Man not mind hitting himself, but still wants to kill the Fly?
options: He believes the Fly deserves punishment regardless of consequences
He distinguishes between accidental self-inflicted pain and the Fly's deliberate harm to him
He thinks his own actions never really hurt him at all
He assumes the Fly caused him to hit himself on purpose

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "derision" mean in "said to him in derision"?
options: Fear or worry
Gratitude or thanks
Mockery or scorn
Confusion or doubt

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Harm done by oneself and harm done by an enemy are judged very differently, even if the pain is the same
Bald men are more vulnerable to insect bites than others
Flies are cleverer than most people give them credit for
Self-inflicted pain is always worse than pain caused by others

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fly do to the Man before he reacts?
options: It buzzes loudly near his ear
It lands on his hand
It flies in circles around his head
It bites him

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Fly describe the Man's own blow to himself?
options: A gentle tap
A heavy smack
A clumsy miss
A painful bruise

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Man accuse the Fly of doing for a living?
options: Spreading disease among animals
Stealing food from houses
Sucking human blood
Waking people up at night

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Man's calm reply undercut the Fly's attempt at mockery?
options: He shows that the pain of the slap does not bother him nearly as much as the Fly assumed
He proves that the slap never actually happened
He admits that he regrets hitting himself after all
He reveals that he was aiming at something else entirely

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Man's willingness to "bear a good deal more" reveal about his priorities?
options: He no longer cares whether the Fly escapes or not
He believes the Fly will eventually apologize to him
He wants to prove he can withstand more pain than the Fly can
He values punishing the Fly more than avoiding pain to himself

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "grudge" mean in "I bear no grudge"?
options: A sudden burst of laughter
A lasting feeling of resentment
A quiet moment of reflection
A formal apology

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Man successfully kills the Fly after several attempts
A Fly convinces the Man to stop trying to kill insects
A Man who hits himself trying to kill a biting Fly explains that hurting himself matters far less than punishing his tormentor
A Man decides the Fly's bite was not worth reacting to at all
